extraction.name: HELVIPAD
extraction.description: A real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation containing 39,553 paired top-bottom images with corresponding depth and disparity maps at 1920 × 512 resolution. It captures dynamic human environments on a university campus, including indoor, outdoor, and nighttime scenes under varied lighting and weather conditions. An augmented training set provides increased label density through automated depth completion.
extraction.creator: Mehdi Zayene; Jannik Endres; Albias Havolli; Charles Corbière; Salim Cherkaoui; Alexandre Kontouli; Alexandre Alahi
extraction.citeAs: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, and Alexandre Alahi. HELVIPAD: A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation. arXiv:2411.18335v2, 25 March 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data were recorded on a university campus using a custom-built remotely controlled robot carrying two vertically arranged Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras and an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR. Cameras captured 3840 × 1920 equirectangular images at 30 fps, while the LiDAR operated at 10 fps with 64 beams and a 42.4° vertical field of view. The camera baseline was 19.1 cm, and the LiDAR was mounted 45 cm below the bottom camera. An NVIDIA Jetson Xavier managed capture, with the LiDAR operating through ROS. A 33 ms external flash and its ROS timestamp supplied a synchronization reference. Scenes included corridors, halls, pedestrian squares, roads, footpaths, and parking areas in daytime and nighttime conditions. The main text reports 29 collected sequences; the supplementary dataset specifications describe 26 included sequences.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Sparse LiDAR measurements leave most image pixels without ground-truth depth labels. Original labels cover approximately 12% of the potentially labelable image region, increasing to approximately 61% after depth completion. The LiDAR's limited vertical field of view restricts labelable rows. Regions with insufficient nearby measurements, such as sky areas, remain unlabeled. Depth completion does not provide labels at some object boundaries. The dataset provides no odometry information.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Paired omnidirectional video streams from two Ricoh Theta V cameras and synchronized 3D point clouds from an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR, recorded from a mobile robot in indoor and outdoor university-campus environments.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The supplementary material states that sequences were captured between December 2023 and February 2024. The sequence table lists recording dates from 2023-12-06 through 2024-01-27.
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: For augmented depth labels, a fully automated pipeline aggregates the current LiDAR point cloud with four preceding and four succeeding clouds without motion transformations. It interpolates radial depth on a spherical grid using an inverse-distance-weighted average of 17 nearest neighbors. Relative weighted variance filters uncertain estimates, with a target ratio of interpolated points of 0.8. An approximately 0.37° average-neighbor-distance threshold excludes regions with insufficient measurements. The pipeline uses 20 million spherical grid points, excludes points outside the LiDAR field of view, and removes completed labels outside each image's original labelable row range. Original labels are retained in ambiguous regions filtered for high uncertainty.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: LiDAR points are transformed into camera coordinates, converted to spherical coordinates, and projected onto bottom-camera equirectangular images. Rotation and translation are optimized by minimizing correspondence errors using BFGS. Spherical disparity is calculated from depth, polar angle, and the camera baseline, and stored in degrees. Temporally aggregated and interpolated point clouds produce an augmented training set. Benchmark experiments also apply photometric augmentation during training.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: During post-processing, flash-blinded frames and corresponding ROS timestamps are identified to align sensor streams. One of every three camera frames is retained to match the LiDAR's 10 fps rate. Images and label maps are cropped to remove unnecessary borders, including sky and ground regions, and downsized. The main text reports a final resolution of 1920 × 512 pixels. Captured sequences are partitioned into training, validation, and test sets while preserving scene-type proportions; test sequences are manually reviewed to ensure no overlap of scenes or areas with training data.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth labels are generated by projecting synchronized LiDAR point clouds onto bottom-camera equirectangular images. At the beginning of recording sessions, key points on a 19 × 19 chessboard are selected in LiDAR scans and matched to image pixel positions to calibrate the transformation. Disparity labels are derived geometrically from depth. Augmented labels are generated by automated temporal aggregation, spherical interpolation, and filtering. Projection accuracy is assessed through manual selection of corresponding LiDAR and image points.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Projection quality is evaluated using Euclidean pixel distances between manually selected corresponding points. The main text reports an average error of 1.7 pixels for 200 randomly selected points and 8.0 pixels for visually challenging locations; supplementary sequence-level assessment reports an overall average of 8.0 pixels, or 0.40% of the image diagonal. Depth-completion hyperparameters are evaluated using an 80–20 split of each measured point cloud. Estimates with high relative weighted variance or insufficient nearby measurements are excluded. The paper notes that this evaluation preferentially samples easier points with nearby measurements, making reported errors lower bounds on errors for uniform image-grid interpolation.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Custom LiDAR-to-equirectangular-image mapping algorithm using BFGS optimization; custom fully automated spherical depth-completion pipeline; geometric depth-to-spherical-disparity conversion.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Images capture pedestrians and human pedestrian activity in university-campus environments. Sequence metadata includes recording dates, time of day, area type, and pedestrian counts.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset supports developing depth-estimation models for navigation and interaction in dynamic human environments. The paper emphasizes evaluating generalization to unseen or underrepresented conditions as necessary for safely deploying learning systems in real-world settings.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Depth labels are concentrated at short ranges, particularly 0–10 meters, partly because the LiDAR captures ground surfaces. Label frequency decreases with increasing depth, which the paper relates to decreasing LiDAR precision at longer distances. Depth completion further enriches the representation of closer objects through interpolation and out-of-distribution filtering. The paper identifies outdoor nighttime conditions as underrepresented. Depth-completion evaluation preferentially samples points with nearby neighbors and therefore underestimates errors associated with uniform image-grid interpolation.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Collection is restricted to a university campus. Depth ground truth is sparse and limited by the LiDAR's vertical field of view. Temporal aggregation is limited for fast-moving objects such as cars. Occlusions are not explicitly handled. Object boundaries may remain unlabeled after completion, and minor measurement discrepancies may occur at boundaries. Sensor synchronization can have up to 16.67 ms of desynchronization. No odometry information is provided. Depth-completion validation errors are lower bounds on image-grid errors because of sampling distribution shift. Models trained only on indoor scenes show limited generalization to outdoor scenes, particularly at night.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, testing, benchmarking, fine-tuning, and pretraining for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation. The dataset is used to compare conventional and omnidirectional stereo models, assess cross-scene and cross-dataset generalization, and evaluate robustness to lighting conditions and depth ranges. Augmented labels are used for training; standard depth and disparity metrics use available sparse ground-truth labels with masking. Depth-completed test maps are used for left-right consistency evaluation because sparse labels rarely occur simultaneously at both image boundaries.
